In addition to submitting a proposed commission structure for purchases completed outside the App Store's in-app purchase (IAP) system in the United States, Apple also filed a motion indicating its willingness to explore a settlement agreement with Epic Games. Details are as follows.

Apple may be ready to settle

Earlier today, Apple submitted a proposal outlining the commissions it hopes to collect on transactions completed through payment systems outside the App Store.

Apple filed this document at the same time the U.S. Supreme Court denied Apple's request. Apple had asked the Supreme Court to stay the lower court proceedings while it sought review of Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers' ruling holding Apple in civil contempt. Apple was found in contempt after continuing to charge a 27% commission even after being ordered by the court to allow developers to steer users to external payment methods.

Under Apple's proposed structure, Apple would be able to collect a maximum 15% commission on transactions completed through alternative payment systems. Epic Games immediately objected, stating it "believes these fees fall well outside the range of permissible fees as guided by the Ninth Circuit."

Although this document has received the most attention, Apple also filed another motion today asking Judge Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties into a settlement conference.

The following is from that document (edited for clarity):

This refers to the fact that Apple's legal team had contacted Epic's attorneys prior to filing the motion to discuss requesting a settlement conference, but Epic did not agree to Apple's request.

Apple argued in the filing that even without Epic's agreement, the court has the authority to order both parties into a settlement conference, adding that the Ninth Circuit itself had encouraged both parties to reach agreement on an appropriate "link-out" commission.

The company also stated that "discussing potential settlement in a confidential, non-adversarial environment will increase the likelihood of reaching a pragmatic resolution that avoids lengthy remand proceedings."

Notably, this document does not contain any specific terms or proposals from Apple regarding a settlement, nor does it constitute an actual settlement offer. Instead, Apple is asking the court to order both parties to conduct settlement negotiations under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.
